---
title: "quarto-index cross-reference conflict probe"
from: markdown-smart
filters:
  - index
---

# Marking one term two different ways

`makeindex` rejects two marks that share an index key and a printed page but
carry different encapsulations, and Quarto turns that rejection into a failed
render. Page numbers do not exist when the filter runs, so it cannot prevent
the clash — it reports it, once per key. This fixture holds one instance of
each shape that clashes, and one that does not.

A plain mark on [kappa]{.index} against a cross-reference three pages below
it. The two plain marks are deliberately on
different printed pages and the cross-reference mark on a third, so the
printed locator count says which marks contributed one: two means the
cross-reference mark contributed none, which is what this extension
documents, and three would mean it did.

{{< pagebreak >}}

The second plain mark on the contested key, a page later: [kappa]{.index}.

{{< pagebreak >}}

The cross-reference mark on the contested key, a page later still:
[kappa]{.index see="Elsewhere"}.

{{< pagebreak >}}

A `see=` on [lambda]{.index see="Here"} against a `see-also=` on
[lambda]{.index see-also="There"}.

A plain mark on [tau]{.index} against a `see-also=` on
[tau]{.index see-also="Elsewhere Again"} — the pairing `kappa` does not
carry, since which attribute is written changes which encapsulation the
back-end emits.

Two `see=` marks naming DIFFERENT targets, which contest the key without
either being a plain mark: [upsilon]{.index see="One Way"} and
[upsilon]{.index see="Another Way"}.

A both-attributes mark, whose single encapsulation is neither a bare `see`
nor a bare `see also`, against a plain mark: [phi]{.index} and
[phi]{.index see="Aye Two" see-also="Bee Two"}.

A contested key BELOW the top level, so the repair is exercised where the
cross-reference hangs off a sub-entry rather than off a top-level term:
[psi]{.index entry="Deep!Level"} and
[omega]{.index entry="Deep!Level" see="Shallow"}.

A contested key whose target carries every character this extension escapes.
Folding a target out of the encapsulation channel and into the entry's
printed text moves it into a field the index tool reads for its own operators
too, so the escaping is probed there and not only where it already was:
[chi]{.index} and
[chi]{.index see="% & # _ { } \\ ~ ^ $ @ | !! \" < >"}.

Two marks that agree, which `makeindex` folds together and which must NOT be
reported: [mu]{.index see="Same"} and [mu]{.index see="Same"}.

A term marked plainly twice, which is the ordinary case and must not be
reported either: [nu]{.index} and [nu]{.index}.

# Cross-reference targets that do and do not resolve

An HTML index links a cross-reference to its target when that target is an
entry in the same index. Whether it is one is decided on the parsed level
list, never on the string a reader sees — and the two can look identical,
since levels are joined with `: ` and a level may contain a colon itself.

A real two-level entry to point at: [pi]{.index entry="Note!on birds"}.

A single-level target that prints exactly like that two-level entry, and must
therefore stay plain text: [rho]{.index see="Note: on birds"}.

The genuine two-level target, which must be a link:
[sigma]{.index see="Note!on birds"}.
